title: Reviewing the alms round
hookLine: after the alms walk, ask: did desire arise on the way?

lines: YOUR FACE IS CLEAR AND BRIGHT.
cards: Sariputta comes out of his solitary sitting one evening in the Bamboo Grove at Rajagaha and goes to the Buddha. Sariputta, the Buddha says, your faculties are clear. Your face is pure and bright.
What have you been abiding in? Emptiness, venerable sir. Good, the Buddha says.
That is the abiding of great people. And then, instead of praising the meditation further, he talks about something ordinary: the morning walk into town to collect food.

teach.h: DID DESIRE ARISE ON THE WAY?
teach.b: A monk who wants to dwell in emptiness, the Buddha says, should look back like this.

On the road I took into the village for alms, in the place where I walked collecting food, on the road I took back: was there any desire, lust, hate, delusion or aversion in my mind toward the things I saw?
The things I heard, smelled, tasted, touched, thought? If he finds there was, he should make an effort to let it go.

teach.h: IF SO, LET IT GO; IF NOT, BE GLAD
teach.b: If there wasn't, he can live with that gladness, training day and night. That's it. A walk, remembered honestly.

The alms round, pindapata, is a walk monks still make today in Theravada countries, bowl in hand, receiving whatever is given. So it's a good test: sights of food, smells from kitchens, people kind and people not.
Then the discourse widens the review into a long checklist. Have I let go of the five strands of sense pleasure? The five hindrances?
Have I understood the five heaps? Developed the foundations of mindfulness, the factors of awakening, the eightfold path? Calm and insight?
Each time, the same two answers: if not yet, keep making effort; if so, rest in that gladness.

teach.h: A WALK REVIEWED, A LIFE MADE CLEAN
teach.b: The title means the purification of almsfood: a walk reviewed this way makes the food, and the life it supports, clean. What's striking is the tone. No guilt, no punishment.
Just an honest look back at the road, and then the next step. And it's taught to Sariputta, whose bright face the Buddha has just praised. Even he is told to check.

how: In Theravada countries monks still walk an alms round, bowl in hand, and looking back over one's actions, taught here and in the earlier advice to Rahula (MN 61), is part of monastic and lay training.

o: a monk's bowl washed after each meal
the alms round, walking to receive food
a vow to fast until the next full moon

games.q: reviewing the alms round: tap the pairs.
p: the alms round, food in the bowl
if desire arose on the way
make an effort to let it go

s: the Buddha tells Sariputta he's beyond needing to review himself
he gives the review practice to Sariputta himself.
the review covers the road there, the place of alms, and the road back
every stretch of the walk, and every sense.
the discourse prescribes a penalty if desire arose
it says simply: make an effort to let it go.

games.q: you're a monk back from the alms round. reviewing the road, you find there was no lust or aversion on the way. what does MN 151 say to do?
o: live with that gladness, training day and night.
walk the route again to be sure.
tell the other monks about it.
games.why: the text allows gladness: if the road was clear, rest in that joy and keep training.

practice: Replay a recent walk slowly, your trip home, to the store, to the kitchen: the door, the street or hallway, what you saw. Did wanting rise somewhere, or irritation, or a fog, and where was it exactly?
If you find something, note it and breathe it out; if you find a stretch that was clear, rest there and be glad.

wordCard.voice: Pindapata. The alms round: looking back honestly at the road you walked, if desire arose, let it go; if not, be glad and keep training. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali pindapata: almsfood, and the alms round that collects it.

carryVoice: Your line: review the road. An ordinary walk, looked at honestly, becomes the practice. Day five hundred sixteen.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 151, Pindapataparisuddhi Sutta (the purification of almsfood)
